lesson.title: Checking the two moves
lesson.skill: Pick the move a two-step equation needs, and say why the order does not change the answer.
lesson.missionLink: You keep choosing the wrong first move and losing the equation halfway. Three questions, three chances to notice it.

primarySource.why: It works both moves one at a time and shows the order each one belongs in.

content.text: Take these three. Nothing is marked, so read every option before you pick one.

questions.prompt: Which step comes first when you solve 2x + 3 = 11?

options.feedback: That is the second move, not the first. It only works once the 3 is off both sides.
Exactly that. Take the 3 off first and the term x is left standing alone.
You cannot divide yet, because there is still a 3 sitting on top of x.

questions.explanation: Undo addition before you undo multiplication. Doing it the other way round changes what the 2 is multiplying.

questions.prompt: Multiplying both sides by one half is the same as which move?

options.feedback: Right size, wrong target. The move has to land on both sides or the equality breaks.
One side only destroys the equality, so that cannot be what it does.
That is it. Multiplying by one half is dividing by two, and it happens to both sides.
The right side is halved along with the left. Both sides always move together.

questions.explanation: Multiplying by one half is dividing by two. It is safe for the same reason every step here is safe: the same operation lands on both sides, so the equality survives.

questions.prompt: Your answer does not check out when you put it back in. What do you check first?

options.feedback: Yes. Every step has to be reversible, or the equation changed meaning somewhere you are not looking.
Whether the answer is a whole number is worth knowing, but it comes after this.
They should match. If they do not, the mistake is earlier than the last line you wrote.

questions.explanation: Check that every step was reversible, then put the answer back on both sides. A mistake in an irreversible step cannot be undone by checking arithmetic.
